passage:
Hi Salma,

You were right to make me talk to the Class 7s. I have been telling everyone about library timings, but on Tuesday at the ground three Class 7 kids told me the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there's a test, and it is never made up. I had never thought of it. So I have changed the speech. New line: "One sports period a week fixed on the timetable, and if it is cancelled, made up within the week." I'll ask the PT teacher whether that is possible before I promise anything. Could you listen to the new version at lunch and time it? It still has to fit in two minutes.

Hemant

qa.q: What did the three Class 7 kids say about sports periods?
qa.a: They said the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there is a test, and it is never made up.

qa.q: What made Hemant change the speech, and how did Hemant feel about it?
qa.a: Hemant was surprised and interested, since Hemant had never thought of the sports periods until the Class 7 kids raised them.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do before promising the schedule, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could ask the PT teacher what is possible, because a promise is only worth making if the person in charge can agree to it.

qa.q: How might a Class 7 student see the new line in the speech?
qa.a: A Class 7 student would likely feel heard, since the complaint they raised on Tuesday became a promise. 🙂

grounding: Mid-campaign, the candidate notices younger students care most about sports periods and revises the speech to include a schedule proposal, showing that listening can reshape a plan in progress.

passage:
You asked what changed my campaign, Jomon? Honestly, a Class 6 kid on the bus.

I'm Vasudha, and three weeks ago my whole speech for sports captain was about new jerseys and an inter-school tournament. Big stuff. I'd practised it maybe twenty times.

Then on the bus this tiny boy asked me, "Didi, will you get us back our games period? They took it for maths revision." And the three kids next to him nodded like it was the only thing in the world.

So I asked around. Class 6, 7, 8, same answer every time. They didn't care about jerseys. They wanted their Thursday games period back.

I rewrote the speech that night. I proposed a timetable where revision moved to zero period twice a week. It meant throwing away twenty rehearsals. But the juniors cheered on the very first line, and I knew I'd listened to the right people.

qa.q: What did the juniors want back?
qa.a: They wanted their Thursday games period back.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when the juniors cheered on the first line?
qa.a: Vasudha felt relieved and confident, sure of having listened to the right people despite throwing away twenty rehearsals.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha do to test the new proposal before the speech?
qa.a: Vasudha could quietly ask a sports teacher whether moving revision to zero period is workable, so the promise is realistic.

qa.q: How might the Class 6 boy on the bus see the new speech?
qa.a: He would probably feel heard and excited, since his one question on the bus shaped the proposal the whole school heard.

grounding: A spoken account of a candidate who notices younger students care about sports periods and revises the speech mid-campaign to include a schedule proposal.

passage:
My name's Joseph, and I sit behind Shalini in 10C, so I watched her campaign for school captain up close.

For the first week, her posters said "Better Labs, Better Results". She gave the same short talk in every class. The seniors nodded. The juniors mostly looked at the clock.

In the second week I saw her standing in the junior block during break with a notebook, talking to Class 6 and 7 kids. She did that three days in a row. I don't know what they said, but she was writing fast.

The next Monday her talk had a new part: a proposal to keep one sports period a week that couldn't be taken for tests. The juniors in our assembly actually cheered. Her posters changed too.

She won. I don't know if that was the reason, but I've never heard juniors cheer for labs.

qa.a: Her posters said "Better Labs, Better Results".

qa.q: What might Shalini have been feeling when the juniors looked at the clock during her early talks?
qa.a: She may have felt uneasy or worried that her message was not reaching the younger students, which could be why she went to talk to them.

qa.q: What else could Shalini have done to learn what juniors wanted?
qa.a: She could have put a simple suggestion box in the junior block, so shy students could answer too.

qa.q: How did the campaign look to Joseph as an observer?
qa.a: To Joseph it looked like a clear turn: after days of listening in the junior block, the talk changed and the juniors cheered, though Joseph cannot be sure that alone won it.

grounding: An observer's account of a candidate noticing juniors care about sports periods and changing the campaign message midway.
